clue.text: Plant containing plant fuel

indicators.note: containing says the first plant's letters hold the second plant inside them

parts.note: cos is a variety of lettuce, so a plant
an alga is a simple water plant

explanation.surface: A power station housing some kind of vegetable fuel source.
explanation.walkthrough: COS is a long-leaved lettuce, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas made from coal was once burnt for heating and lighting, a fuel in its own right.

clue.text: Backing release from prison, cue ugliest extremists, doubly stir crazy

indicators.note: crazy says all these letters go wild into a new order
doubly says those two outer letters are used twice
extremists, read as the extreme letters, takes the first and last of ugliest

explanation.surface: Support for a prisoner's release, with a nasty cue and doubly crazy stirring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of ugliest, UT, taken doubly give UTUT; with PRISON, CUE and STIR they make the anagram. 'Stir' is prison slang, but here it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin term names withdrawal before climax, a pulling back of release, as a contraceptive method.

clue.text: Song C, then ___ for spice?

parts.note: the missing word after C makes a spice; the Beatles song title supplies the line that this word alone is required

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank prompt: a letter, then a gap, for a cooking spice.
explanation.walkthrough: C followed by LOVE gives CLOVE; the Beatles song title says that word is all C requires.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beatles' 1967 single title literally says a single word is the only requirement.

clue.text: Article supporting a crossword setter in bloody competitive strategy

indicators.note: in says the whole group sits inside the bloody word

parts.note: gory means bloody

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting puts the article underneath the setter

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A grammar article backs a crossword setter in a vicious contest of tactics.
explanation.definitionFit: The mathematical study of strategic decisions between competing players models rival strategies.

clue.text: Hat has shifted right up

indicators.note: shifted says the three letters of has are moved about
up in a down clue says the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: OK means all right

explanation.surface: Someone's hat has slipped right up on their head.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall cylindrical military cap with a peak and plume is a type of headgear.

clue.text: Novel instrument ends in celesta

parts.note: a rebec is a medieval stringed instrument played with a bow

indicators.note: ends in says take only the two outermost letters of the word celesta

explanation.surface: An unusual musical instrument whose sound ends in a celesta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective for the instrument but is the definition: a famous book title.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphne du Maurier's 1938 book of that title is a well-known Gothic novel.

clue.text: Transmitter taking so long to receive mother in outskirts of Rabat

indicators.note: in says the farewell group sits between those outer letters
outskirts of takes the outer letters of Rabat
to receive says the farewell word takes in the mother word

parts.note: adios is Spanish for goodbye, so long
ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: A broadcaster taking ages to welcome mother on the edge of the Moroccan capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall broadcasting tower sends out radio signals, so it is a transmitter.

clue.text: Personal problem needs time for Danish physicist

parts.note: BO is body odour, a personal hygiene problem
HR is the abbreviation for hour, a unit of time

explanation.surface: A private issue needs time to resolve for a Scandinavian scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: Niels Bohr was the Danish Nobel physicist who modelled the atom's structure.

clue.text: Visitor about to enter data source

indicators.note: about says the visitor word goes round the entering word

parts.note: a comer is someone who comes, a visitor
to put data in is to enter it

explanation.surface: A guest is about to come into a place of information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads like 'on the point of', but 'about' is the container signal and 'to enter' gives PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A computing machine stores and supplies information, so it is a source of data.

clue.text: Sheer muscles overcoming minstrel's invocation?

indicators.note: in a down clue, overcoming puts the muscles above the invocation

parts.note: abs are abdominal muscles
a minstrel might address his instrument as O lute

explanation.surface: Pure muscle overpowering a wandering singer's appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O' is the poetic vocative, as in addressing someone: a minstrel might cry 'O lute!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheer and absolute both mean complete or utter, as in sheer folly.

clue.text: M. Ali's conversion — was to this?

definitions.text: M. Ali's conversion — was to this?

indicators.note: conversion signals that the letters of the name are converted into a new order

parts.note: the initial and surname plus the S give five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Muhammad Ali's famous change of faith: was this the religion he turned to?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the boxer did convert to this faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Muhammad Ali became a Muslim in the 1960s, so the faith he converted to fits the whole clue.

clue.text: See 22
All may see the point, nothing to accomplish with unknown maverick

parts.note: U is the British film certificate for Universal, suitable for all audiences
north is a point of the compass
O looks like zero, nothing
to do is to accomplish
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: An oddball tries to get everyone to see the point, achieving nothing with someone unknown.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film rating meaning anyone may watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A maverick is an independent thinker who goes against convention, which is an unconventional person.

clue.text: Some ship in port

definitions.meaning: the body or frame of a vessel, one part of the boat
a city and port on the Humber estuary in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Part of a vessel sitting in harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' does not signal hidden letters here: the main body of a vessel is some of the ship. Hull is an English port city on the Humber.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of a boat is one part of it, and the Yorkshire city is a major seaport.

clue.text: Twitter feeding county working for old London borough

indicators.note: feeding says the bird word goes into the county

parts.note: Kent is the county in south-east England
to twitter like a bird is to sing
on means working, operating

explanation.surface: Social media posts feeding a county's work for a historic part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitter' suggests the social network, but means birdsong. Kent is a county south-east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Kensington was a metropolitan borough until 1965, when it merged with Chelsea.

clue.text: Kinky man with ten elves in bondage

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A man with a fetish joined by ten elves in a bondage session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kinky' and 'bondage' share a racy surface, but the definition means slavery.
explanation.definitionFit: Bondage in its old sense is the state of being a slave, held in servitude.

clue.text: Extra large number one wrote in Swiss town

indicators.note: in says the pen goes inside the town's name

parts.note: Sion is a town in the Valais canton of Switzerland
a quill is a feather pen, something one wrote with

explanation.surface: A huge number of people wrote in from a Swiss town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one wrote' reads as a person, but is the writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular word for a vast unspecified quantity, an enormous figure.

clue.text: Cyrano de Bergerac was playing God with Ibsen

indicators.note: playing says the letters of these words act out a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The famous French character was performing deity alongside the Norwegian playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostand's swordsman hero is famous for his huge nose, which he is mocked for.

clue.text: Flipping Vietnam War T-shirt claims no hero

indicators.note: Flipping says the hidden letters are read backwards
claims means takes in, so the phrase holds the letters within it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A flippant Vietnam War T-shirt declares that nobody is a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'claims no hero' as the definition, but 'claims' is the hidden-word signal (the phrase claims the letters), leaving 'no hero' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of straw is a weak, ineffectual figure, the opposite of a brave champion.

clue.text: See 1 down
Middle East city where live wire cuts all borders off

parts.note: to be is to live, exist

indicators.note: all borders off says strip the first and last letters from both wire and cuts

explanation.surface: A city where a live electric cable cuts off every frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'live wire' looks like one phrase, an energetic person, but 'live' and 'wire' do separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Lebanon lies on the eastern Mediterranean, a city of the Middle East.

clue.text: See 2
Cool without water etc

definitions.meaning: a spirit served undiluted, with no water or ice

explanation.surface: A cool drink served with no water added and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for excellent, and the barroom term for a spirit taken undiluted.

clue.text: 10 usually handled carelessly

definitions.meaning: the usual count of human digits on two hands is ten

explanation.surface: Ten things normally treated without care.
explanation.walkthrough: Most people have eight fingers and two thumbs, ten digits in all; the phrase is also an idiom for clumsiness.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone clumsy who fumbles everything they touch, and literally counts the ten digits.

clue.text: Extra large number?

definitions.meaning: a shirt size, and XL is the Roman numeral for this figure

explanation.surface: A question: is extra large a figure?
explanation.walkthrough: XL, the label for extra large, is also the Roman numeral for this number.
explanation.definitionFit: XL stands both for a big clothing size and, in Roman numerals, for four tens.

clue.text: See 2
Expert waiting for someone prostrate in the trenches of northern France?

parts.note: the Somme was the First World War battlefield of trenches in northern France
a lier is someone who lies down flat

explanation.surface: An expert waits for someone lying in the First World War trenches.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whimsically, a 'lier' in the 'Somme' is someone prostrate in the trenches; 'Expert waiting' is the definition, not someone waiting for a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine waiter in a restaurant is an expert in wine who waits at tables.

clue.text: Body's virtual middle (approximately)

indicators.note: middle says take the central letter of the seven-letter word virtual

parts.note: or so means approximately, roughly

explanation.surface: The body's near-central part, give or take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body's' is the definition with 's as is; 'virtual middle' looks like part of the definition, but it is the centre letter of virtual.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk of the human frame, without head or limbs, is the main body.

clue.text: Antipodean port's riot on the beach?

indicators.note: on in an across clue puts the word for riot after the beach word

parts.note: a dune is a sand hill by the beach
a din is a loud noise, a riot of sound

explanation.surface: A port down under has a disturbance on the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: Antipodean refers to Australia and New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: The city in New Zealand's South Island has a harbour, so it is a southern hemisphere port.

clue.text: Following positive principle, I'm out of time rounding double bend, as a long-distance runner

indicators.note: following means the rest comes after the principle

parts.note: yang is the positive, active principle in Chinese philosophy

indicators.note: rounding says the remaining letters go round the bend letter
out of says those two letters are taken out of the word time

parts.note: taken as written
the letters of I'm, without the apostrophe
a Z has the shape of a double bend, as on a road sign

explanation.surface: After a positive principle, I'm out of time going round a double bend like a marathon runner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' leaves TE from TIME, and 'rounding' wraps TE around Z. 'Runner' looks like an athlete but is a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river runs, and China's great river flows for thousands of kilometres.
